```{python}
#| label: setup
#| output: false
# Every number and figure on this page is read from the stored results in
# data/02-analysis_data. No language model is called when the page is built.
import importlib.util
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
from IPython.display import HTML, display

ROOT = Path("..")


def load_script(name, file):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, ROOT / "scripts" / file)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module


si = load_script("si", "08-silicon_views.py")
query = load_script("query", "03-query_models.py")
sd = si.load(ROOT)
summary, seats = sd["summary"], sd["seats"]
ctrl = si.control_stats(seats)
rep_favoured = int((summary["p_rep_win"] >= 0.5).sum())
costs = si.cost_table(sd["resp"])
ind_shares = si.independents_shares(sd)
cmp = si.compare_with_regression(summary, ROOT)
n_agree = int((cmp["call"] != "Methods disagree").sum())
bt_stats = sd["bt"].group_by("model").agg(
    bias=pl.col("error").mean() * 100, mae=pl.col("error").abs().mean() * 100, right=pl.col("winner_right").sum()
)
calib = {r["model"]: r for r in sd["calib"].iter_rows(named=True)}


def share(df, source, side):
    row = df[(df["source"] == source) & (df["side"] == side)]
    return f"{100 * row['share'].iloc[0]:.0f}%" if len(row) else "0%"
```

::: {.write}
Opening paragraph (2 to 3 sentences): what this page is and that every "voter" is synthetic. Then the headline:
Republicans keep the Senate in **`{python} f"{100 * ctrl['p_rep_control']:.0f}%"`** of 10,000 simulated elections,
median **`{python} f"{ctrl['median']:.0f}"`** Republican seats (80% interval `{python} f"{ctrl['lo']:.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{ctrl['hi']:.0f}"`). Republicans are favoured in `{python} str(rep_favoured)` of 35 races.
:::

## How the forecast is built {#method}

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(si.pipeline_html())
```

::: {.write}
One short paragraph per step, in order: (1) personas from real CES 2024 respondents [@kuriwaki2025]; (2) the prompt,
following @argyle2023 and @bisbee2024; (3) three models through OpenRouter, five answers each at temperature 1;
(4) weights: survey weight times midterm turnout estimated from CES 2022; (5) calibration with the 2024 line;
(6) the simulation, with its four sources of uncertainty (national swing of 3 points, an assumption; state error of
4.7 points, measured leave-one-out; which model; sampling). Ballots from @wiki2026.
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
races26 = {r["state"]: r for r in sd["races_2026"].iter_rows(named=True)}
example = pl.read_parquet(ROOT / "data" / "02-analysis_data" / "personas_2026.parquet").filter(
    pl.col("state") == "OH"
).sample(1, seed=853).row(0, named=True)
prompt = query.build_prompt(example["backstory"], races26["OH"], 2026)
print(f'<div class="prompt-box"><b>System:</b> {query.SYSTEM_PROMPT}\n\n<b>User:</b> {prompt}</div>')
```

::: {.write}
One sentence introducing the prompt above (a real Ohio persona, shown exactly as sent). Mention the forced-choice
follow-up for pure independents (section 4).
:::

## Does it work? The 2024 backtest {#backtest}

::: {.write}
We ran the same pipeline on 2024, when the answers are known: 4,833 personas in 33 races, with models whose knowledge
ends before that election. Before calibration the models are too Democratic (bias
`{python} f"{bt_stats.filter(model='GPT-4o mini')['bias'][0]:.1f}"` points for GPT-4o mini,
`{python} f"{bt_stats.filter(model='Llama 3.3 70B')['bias'][0]:.1f}"` for Llama) and too extreme: the calibration
slopes are `{python} f"{calib['GPT-4o mini']['slope']:.2f}"` and `{python} f"{calib['Llama 3.3 70B']['slope']:.2f}"`,
so real results are about two thirds as lopsided as the synthetic ones. Link to @bisbee2024.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-backtest
#| fig-cap: "2024 backtest. Each dot is one of the 33 Senate races of 2024: the synthetic voters' Republican share (before calibration) against the actual result [@wiki2024]. The dashed line is a perfect forecast; the solid line is the calibration line fitted to these races and used to correct the 2026 forecast. The three largest misses for each model are labelled."
si.fig_backtest(sd["bt"], sd["calib"])
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-agreement
#| fig-cap: "Person by person in 2024: the share of synthetic voters who pick the same side (Republican or opposition) as the real respondent reported voting, by party identification. The party-line baseline simply has everyone vote with their party, so it has no prediction for pure independents."
si.fig_by_party(sd["by_party"])
```

::: {.write}
The key finding at the individual level: for partisans the models are no better than knowing party identification
(about 94% for both models and the baseline on the same people). Pure independents are where the models are weakest
(about 65%), as @argyle2023 also found.
:::

## The independents problem {#independents}

```{python}
#| label: fig-independents
#| fig-cap: "The 711 pure independents in the 2024 backtest. Free answer: what the models said when asked how the persona voted. Forced answer: what they said when asked to choose between the Republican and the main opponent. Real vote: what the same respondents reported (351 who reported a two-party vote). All shares use CES survey weights."
si.fig_independents(ind_shares)
```

::: {.write}
Asked freely, the models give `{python} share(ind_shares, "Free answer", "Other")` of pure independents' answers to
"Other". Forced to choose, they send them to the opposition (`{python} share(ind_shares, "Forced answer", "Opposition")`),
while the same people reported voting `{python} share(ind_shares, "Real vote", "Republican")` Republican. Explain why we
used the forced choice anyway and that it is the same in 2024 and 2026. Connect to mode collapse in @heath2026.
:::

## Second opinions {#second-opinions}

### A regression forecast

::: {.write}
Two or three sentences on the regression: a ridge regression of each state's Senate vote on its lagged demographics and
partisanship, 2014 to 2024, checked against certified results. The full write-up and code are in the repository
(`paper/_regression.qmd`, `scripts/05-regression.py`). The two methods name the same winner in
`{python} str(n_agree)` of 35 races.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-regression
#| fig-cap: "Silicon sampling against the regression, one dot per 2026 race. Red and blue dots are races where both methods favour the same side; hollow dots are races where they disagree. The regression's share is the Republican share of the two-party vote."
si.fig_vs_regression(cmp)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy on the 33 Senate races of 2024, out of sample for both methods: the silicon rows are the raw synthetic estimates (no model was fitted to 2024), and the regression was not trained on 2024. Average miss is in percentage points of the two-party vote."
display(HTML(si.booktabs(si.accuracy_table(sd["bt"], ROOT), ["Average miss (points)", "Winners called"])))
```

### Do the models agree?

```{python}
#| label: fig-models
#| fig-cap: "Raw Republican share by race from each model's synthetic voters, before calibration. Only GPT-4o mini and Llama 3.3 70B were backtested on 2024 and feed the forecast; DeepSeek V4 Flash knows about 2025 and 2026 but cannot be backtested, so it is shown for comparison only."
si.fig_models(summary)
```

::: {.write}
What the comparison shows: the three models land close together, and DeepSeek is more Democratic in most competitive
races. What that might mean (it knows the 2026 political environment, the older models do not).
:::

## Uncertainty, costs and limits {#limits}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-costs
#| tbl-cap: "Every model call made for this project, through OpenRouter. The first 2026 run is included although DeepSeek's answers from it were unusable (its reasoning used up the reply limit) and were replaced by the rerun."
display(HTML(si.booktabs(costs, ["Models", "Replies", "Cost (US$)"])))
```

::: {.write}
Discussion, connecting to the literature:
@argyle2023 (algorithmic fidelity; independents), @bisbee2024 (too little variance, exaggerated differences: our slope
of about 0.63), @heath2026 (mode collapse; our "Other" answers), @gelman2020 (correlated errors, the national swing as
an assumption, rounding probabilities).
Limits: one calibration election, from a presidential year; the 3-point national swing is assumed; candidates are
described by party only; no 2026 survey; three-way races (Maine 2024, Montana and Mississippi 2026) are measured
against the combined opposition. Where the forecast disagrees with expert ratings (Massachusetts, Illinois, Michigan,
Ohio, Nebraska, Alaska) and why. Total cost: US$`{python} f"{costs.attrs['total_cost']:.2f}"`.
:::

## Software and data {.unnumbered}

Analysis in Python [@citePython] with uv [@citeUv], Polars [@citePolars], pandas [@citePandas], NumPy [@citeNumpy],
PyArrow [@citeArrow], scikit-learn [@citeScikit], plotnine [@citePlotnine] and Matplotlib [@citeMatplotlib]; site

[@kuriwaki2025]; candidates and results from @wiki2026 and @wiki2024.
